This guide explains how to build a causal graph and what each graph class means.
For a full introduction to these graphs and the theory behind them, see, for
instance, @pearl2009causality or @peters2017elements;
@richardsonspirtes2002ancestral cover ancestral graphs (AGs and MAGs)
specifically, and @zhang2008completeness covers PAGs.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(CausalStructures)
```

## Constructing graphs

`cgraph()` builds a graph from edges written with infix operators, and its
`class` argument (`"DAG"` by default) sets the graph class:

```{r}
dag <- cgraph(A %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y)
admg <- cgraph(X %-->% Y, X %<->% Y, class = "ADMG")
```

Each operator is an edge with a mark at either end: a tail (`-`), an arrowhead
(`<` or `>`) or a circle (`o`).

  | Operator | Edge                                |
  | :------- | :---------------------------------- |
  | `%-->%`  | directed, `src --> dst`             |
  | `%<--%`  | directed, `dst --> src`             |
  | `%---%`  | undirected                          |
  | `%<->%`  | bidirected                          |
  | `%o->%`  | partially directed, `src o-> dst`   |
  | `%<-o%`  | partially directed, `dst o-> src`   |
  | `%o--%`  | partially undirected, `src o-- dst` |
  | `%--o%`  | partially undirected, `dst o-- src` |
  | `%o-o%`  | partial (circles at both ends)      |

`+` fans an edge out to (or in from) several nodes at once, and chaining
operators connects consecutive groups of nodes, so `A %-->% B %-->% C` gives the
two edges `A --> B` and `B --> C`, while `A %-->% B + C` gives `A --> B` and
`A --> C`. A bare node name declares an isolated node:

```{r}
nodes(cgraph(A %-->% B, F))
```

To build a graph from a string made at run time, pass the same edges as a string
through `spec`, with the operators written without `%`:

```{r}
spec <- paste("A -->", paste0("X", 1:3, collapse = " + "))
edges(cgraph(spec = spec))
```

## Graph classes

Each class is checked on construction, so a graph of a class is always valid for
it. Building a DAG with a cycle, or with a bidirected edge, is an error:

```{r}
#| error: true

cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C %-->% A)
cgraph(A %<->% B)
```

`reclass()` changes the class of an existing graph, again checking the result,
and the predicates (`is_dag()`, `is_cpdag()`, `is_mag()`, ...) test whether a
graph satisfies a class's constraints, independent of its own graph class.

### Directed acyclic graphs

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is the standard causal graph. All edges are
directed (`-->`), and the graph contains no directed cycles. An edge `X --> Y`
means `X` is a direct cause of `Y`.

### Partially directed acyclic graphs

The PDAG family (`"PDAG"`, `"CPDAG"`, `"MPDAG"`) has directed (`-->`) and
undirected (`---`) edges, and no directed cycles. An undirected edge is one
whose orientation is not specified.

- A **PDAG** is the general case.
- A **CPDAG** represents a whole Markov equivalence class of DAGs: an edge stays
  undirected exactly when its orientation varies across the class. It is what
  constraint-based causal discovery algorithms such as PC estimate from
  observational data, and `dag_to_cpdag()` computes it from a DAG.
- An **MPDAG** is a CPDAG with background knowledge added, which may orient
  edges the equivalence class alone leaves undetermined.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

plot(dag_to_cpdag(dag))
```

See [Equivalence Classes](equivalence-classes.qmd) for worked examples of all
three.

### Acyclic directed mixed graphs

An ADMG (acyclic directed mixed graph) has directed (`-->`) and bidirected
(`<->`) edges. Directed edges are causal relations, while a bidirected edge is
unobserved confounding between its endpoints. An ADMG is, for example, what
`latent_project()` gives when it projects latent variables out of a DAG:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

full <- cgraph(U %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y)
plot(latent_project(full, "U"))
```

### Ancestral graphs

Ancestral graphs (`"AG"` and its maximal subclass `"MAG"`) have directed
(`-->`), bidirected (`<->`) and undirected (`---`) edges. In an ancestral graph,
an arrowhead at a node means that node is not an ancestor of the other endpoint.
A bidirected edge thus means neither endpoint is an ancestor of the other; in
causal applications such edges commonly represent unobserved confounding.

Undirected edges mean something different here than in a PDAG: rather than an
unknown orientation, they represent **selection bias**, associations arising
from conditioning on variables that are common effects. A MAG is the ancestral
graph of a DAG with latent and selection variables marginalized and conditioned
out, and is maximal: every pair of non-adjacent nodes can be separated.

### Partial ancestral graphs

A PAG plays the role for MAGs that a CPDAG plays for DAGs: it represents a
Markov equivalence class of MAGs [@zhang2008completeness], and is what the FCI
algorithm estimates. PAG edges can have three endpoint marks: a tail, an
arrowhead or a circle, and a circle means that mark is not the same in every MAG
in the class. `mag_to_pag()` computes the PAG of a MAG:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

mag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B, B %-->% D, class = "MAG")
plot(mag_to_pag(mag))
```

See [PAG Causal Effects](pag-causal-effects.qmd) for estimating causal effects
from a PAG.

### Undirected graphs

A UG (`"UG"`) has only undirected (`---`) edges. Undirected graphs are not
common in causal inference, but are available for those who need them; for
example, `moralize()` returns one.

### Unknown graphs

`"UNKNOWN"` imposes no structural constraints. It accepts every edge type,
including self-loops and parallel edges, for graphs that do not fit any other
class:

```{r}
edges(cgraph(A %-->% B, A %<->% B, B %-->% B, class = "UNKNOWN"))
```

## Background knowledge

Sometimes you know some causal relations in advance: `A` must cause `B`, or `C`
does not cause `D`. `apply_background_knowledge()` adds such knowledge to a
PDAG, required edges as `%-->%` (or `%<--%`) and forbidden ones as `%!-->%` (or
`%!<--%`), and propagates the orientations it implies, giving an MPDAG:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

cpdag <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C, class = "CPDAG")
plot(apply_background_knowledge(cpdag, A %-->% B))
```

`dag_to_mpdag()` does the same starting from a DAG, using its CPDAG.
